summary: Defines the CBOR Sequence format, which is simply any number of encoded CBOR data items concatenated one after another, along with the media type application/cbor-seq. It also describes a structured syntax suffix so other media types can declare that they build on this format.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of a string of beads where each bead is a small piece of data. This says you can just thread them one after another without needing a box around them.

questions: what is the application/cbor-seq media type
how do you decode a cbor sequence
subtitle: Glue CBOR data items end to end and you have a sequence, with no separators or end marker needed.

tldr.problem: Sometimes you want a stream or file of many CBOR values that can be concatenated or grown at the end by appending, without wrapping everything in one array or needing a streaming CBOR parser.
tldr.mechanism: A CBOR Sequence is zero or more encoded CBOR data items simply concatenated. Items are self delimiting, so no separator is needed. The RFC also registers the application/cbor-seq media type and the +cbor-seq structured syntax suffix.
tldr.outcome: Sequences can be produced and consumed incrementally. The format has no end-of-sequence marker and no integrity protection, and a malformed item makes the rest of the sequence undecodable.

today: RFC 8742 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Sequences of CBOR Items
sections.content:
The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR, RFC 7049) serializes data in the JSON data model or in its own somewhat expanded model. When you serialize a sequence of such values, it is sometimes convenient to simply concatenate them, or to append more items to a sequence that grows at the end.

RFC 8742 describes CBOR Sequences, made of zero or more encoded CBOR data items. They can be consumed and produced incrementally, without a streaming CBOR parser that delivers parts of an item early or an encoder that emits parts of an item incrementally. The RFC also defines the application/cbor-seq media type and the +cbor-seq structured syntax suffix.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you have lots of little notes and want to keep adding more to the end of the pile. This RFC says how to stack CBOR notes so you can just keep adding.

sections.title: The CBOR Sequence Format
sections.content:
A CBOR Sequence is defined recursively. It is either an empty (zero-length) sequence of bytes, or the bytes of one encoded CBOR data item followed by a CBOR Sequence. Concatenating zero or more encoded items makes a sequence, and concatenating sequences makes another sequence.

There is no end-of-sequence indicator. If you want one, the RFC suggests encoding an array of the values as a single CBOR data item instead.

Unlike JSON Text Sequences (RFC 7464), CBOR Sequences use no marker between items. That works because CBOR data items are self delimiting, so the end of each can always be calculated.
sections.plainLanguage: Each bead tells you how big it is, so you do not need a divider between beads. The string just ends when the beads run out.

sections.title: Decoding and Truncation
sections.content:
Decoding is simple. An empty byte sequence gives an empty sequence of values. Otherwise, decode one data item from the front, put its value first in the result, and repeat on the remaining bytes. A streaming decoder can hand over each value as soon as its bytes have arrived.

The consequence is that if any item is not well formed, the rest of the sequence cannot be reliably decoded. Handling malformed data is outside the scope of the specification.

The format can detect truncation of the last item, and a streaming decoder may simply pause for more data. It cannot detect data items that are entirely missing at the end.
sections.plainLanguage: You read one bead, then the next. If a bead is broken in the middle, you cannot tell where the next one starts. If beads are missing off the end, you will not notice.

sections.title: The +cbor-seq Suffix
sections.content:
Media types can use a structured syntax suffix to say which media type they build on. RFC 7049 already defines +cbor. RFC 8742 defines +cbor-seq.

A media type SHOULD use +cbor-seq when parsing its bytes as a CBOR Sequence is meaningful and is at least sometimes not just a single CBOR data item. Media types that always carry a single item should keep using +cbor.

Applications seeing such a type can use generic processing, or use generic CBOR Sequence tools for the first parse and add their own processing on top.
sections.plainLanguage: A suffix is a label on the box that says what it is made from. This one says that the box holds a string of CBOR beads.

sections.title: Practical Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC gives three pieces of practical advice.

  • CDDL. The CDDL notation (RFC 8610) supports sequences inside byte strings through the .cborseq control operator. For a top-level sequence, describe an array in CDDL and say in English text that the specification is really about a sequence of the array's elements.
  • Diagnostic notation. Enclose the items in an array, as in [1, 2, 3]. In informal settings the outer brackets can be left off, as in 1, 2, 3. Zero-length sequences are hard to discuss in the second form.
  • Skipping elements. If you need to skip an element without decoding it, or fan elements out to multiple decoding threads, use CBOR byte strings that contain embedded CBOR as the elements. Byte strings carry their length.

With byte-string elements, you may also be able to recover from an element that is not well formed inside, as long as the sequence of byte strings is well formed.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to skip a bead quickly, put it in a small labeled bag that says how big it is. Then you can pass over the bag without opening it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of CBOR apply. The format gives no cryptographic integrity protection, but can be combined with CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE, RFC 8152). COSE can protect a whole sequence or each element on its own. In the second case, extra effort may be needed to protect the relationship between elements.

Decoders must assume input is untrusted, and MUST fail gracefully on malicious input.
sections.plainLanguage: The string of beads has no lock on it. If you want to be sure nobody changed it, you need to add a seal separately.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has registered three things.

  • The media type application/cbor-seq, with encoding considerations of binary and intended usage COMMON.
  • A CoAP Content-Format ID of 63 for that media type, from the Expert Review (0-255) range.
  • The +cbor-seq structured syntax suffix. Fragment identifiers for it SHOULD follow those of application/cbor-seq, and the text notes that no fragment identification syntax is defined for that type.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA wrote the new name and a number into the official lists so everyone uses the same ones.
